title: Inquest looks into death
article: It may not be goodbye, but for the family of David Troy Stevens who died in police custody in 2008, the completion of an inquest into his death at least provides some closure and comfort that they at least knowing what happened to their loved one.
The inquest was held on Tuesday and Wednesday (Aug. 3 and 4) in Lindsay and was presided over by Dr. Peter Clark, regional supervising coroner for East Region, Peterborough office.

Eight witnesses were put on the stand to testify what they saw June 8, 2008 at the Admiral Inn and Convention Centre on Highway 7. Court heard that Mr. Stevens, 27, was staying at the inn and sometime in the early morning hours became agitated, banging on walls and doors and breaking things in his room on the second floor.
Jurors heard from another guest who was in a room close to Mr. Stevens' that night about the excessive noise he was making as well as from the front desk clerk who originally called the police.

Jurors also heard from the three Kawartha Lakes Police officers who responded to the rather vague call of a man making noise and possibly hurting himself about 2:25 a.m. The first two responding officers waited for a short time for a third - Sgt. Harry Hughes - officer to arrive, for police safety, testified Const. Brendan Johnston.
"I was familiar with him because police had dealt with him on several times prior...he had a tendency to be violent and anti-police," he said.

Court heard that when officers went into Mr. Stevens' room it was in disarray and darkness because the lights were smashed, with a broken toilet flooding water in the bathroom and blood on the walls and floor, but Mr. Stevens was not there. When police located Mr. Stevens a short time later in a room he had broken into on the first floor, Const. Johnston said he saw something he will never forget.

"I've never seen anything like it before in my life, his eyes were crazed," he said of Mr. Stevens who was crouched in the corner in darkness, as the lights of the second room had been smashed as well.

Const. Alex McMillan concurred with Const. Johnston's assessment of Mr. Stevens, adding that he was ranting and not making any sense and for the first few moments in the room with the man, he wasn't even sure Mr. Stevens was aware he wasn't alone. The officers said Mr. Stevens had blood on his hands and head from what appeared to be superficial cuts, even though Mr. Stevens was yelling that he had been shot in the head.
"I noticed that his pupils were huge - like saucers - he looked like a wild animal," Const, McMillan said.
"It was obvious that he had ingested something," he added of Mr. Stevens' behaviour.

After a short time, the police officers testified that Mr. Stevens did comply and with only a little resistance, let himself be handcuffed. Officers testified they promptly moved Mr. Stevens to a sitting position, because "his breathing didn't sound right," said Sgt. Hughes. Then, Mr. Stevens took several deep breathes and seemed to hold them, before slumping over. The officers testified that they immediately took off the handcuffs and once they could not find a pulse, commenced CPR, with Const. McMillan doing chest compressions and Const. Johnston breathing into Mr. Stevens' mouth with a protective mask.

The final witness to take the stand, Len van Pelt, an advanced care paramedic with Kawartha Lakes EMS, said when he and his partner arrived at the inn about 3 a.m. they found police officers performing CPR. Upon assessment, Mr. van Pelt said Mr. Stevens was vital signs absent (VSA) and had no heart rhythm at all so a defibrillator could not be used. Lifesaving techniques were implemented as quickly as possible given the only available light was from flashlights, Mr. van Pelt testified. Once paramedics got an IV into Mr. Stevens, they administered six doses of two different kinds of medication as well as some saline solution over the next 30 minutes in an effort to save his life. After consulting with the base hospital doctor, Mr. van Pelt, said one last medication was tried to no avail.
Mr. Stevens was pronounced dead at the scene at 3:37 a.m.

Dr. Daryl Mayers a toxicologist from the Centre of Forensic Sciences, who tested samples of Mr. Stevens' blood and urine, was able to find cocaine, a break-down product of cocaine, which indicates more than one cocaine administration leading up to the medical emergency, morphine and methadone.

"I detected the presence of cocaine in a concentration of 0.75 milligrams per litre of blood," he said, adding that while he could not conclusively say it was the cause of death in his role as a toxicologist, "It was certainly well within the range that could cause toxicity."
He went on to explain that cocaine has effects on the brain and heart, particularly increasing the heart rate and blood pressure and constricting the blood vessels, he said.
"It has the potential to cause cardiac arrest or heart attacks."

Chief pathologist for Ontario Dr. Michael Pollanen found the cause of death to be "acute cocaine intoxication," in the autopsy report completed the day following the death provided as an exhibit in court.

Mr. Stevens' best friend, Brent Henderson, testified that Mr. Stevens was visiting the area from Alberta at the time of his death, and one of the reasons he had come was to get connected with a methadone program to try to kick his drug habit. Mr. Stevens had already been through the initial steps toward a methadone routine, Mr. Henderson said, and was supposed to get picked up by Mr. Henderson's brother the morning he died to visit the clinic again.

Before the jury went out, Dr. Clark explained that a death inquest is not designed to assign any blame or guilt, but rather to fully examine the death to clarify circumstances as well as assure the public that nothing was overlooked and examine whether something could be learned that would prevent similar deaths in the future.

A jury of five people, three women and two men, was required to answer the following questions: who died, when they died, where they died, how they died and by what means did they come to their death. On top of answering the pertinent questions, jurors also had the opportunity to make recommendations about how similar deaths could be avoided in the future. Jury decisions need not be unanimous, explained Dr. Clark, a majority decision is sufficient. Jurors also do not need to have the case proven beyond a reasonable doubt. The standard of proof in the case of death inquests is a balance of probabilities, the coroner explained. Beyond the basic facts of the case, jurors found the death to be accidental and declined to make recomendations.
The inquest was mandatory under the Corners Act of Ontario as the death happened while Mr. Stevens was in police custody.
The son, brother and father to eight and four-year-old girls will be sorely missed by his family.

Members of his family flew from his native New Brunswick to attend the inquest, and said the outcome was basically what they expected. Mr. Stevens' sister, Melissa Garnett, said she had hoped for some sort of recommendation that an ambulance should be called as soon as there was any indication of injury, like in her brother's case when the initial call came to police that there was possibly someone hurting himself. Ms Garnett said if an ambulance had been called earlier, maybe paramedics would have been on scene when her brother's heart stopped and he would have had a better chance for survival, a sentiment shared by her mother, Marsha Kingston.

For Ms Kingston, it is a comfort to finally know without question what exactly happened on that night. But instead of focusing on her son's death, she said she would like to remember the man he was. Those close to him described him as a funny and generous guy who would give you the shirt off his back.
"He was a good boy...he was kind to everybody," she said.
